You have to remember this was a different time. During the peak of the first browser wars there was many changes happening on every front. IE was king at the time because it was widely distributed and offered many more technical features than Netscape or Opera at the time. I was a younger programmer then coming into my experience power curve in the late 90s. I worked with most of the Microsoft browser and development technologies of the time because I needed to build powerful applications and systems for the corporation I was working for. I introduced them to corporate intranet technology and spent six years growing that intranet to do so many things. Netscape was a decent browser for surfing the web, but it was growth stunted by its limited support of technologies that were needed for building strong web apps. They relied too much on a 3rd party plugin ecosystem that was in its infancy. Microsoft, on the other hand, was delivering something new at least every month. IE got ActiveX (and COM) technology that enabled developers to build desktop-style apps that could be delivered by the browser. The Office suite of products got their ActiveX viewers (which is part of what I believe is referred to by Bill here). Active Server Pages and Active Data Objects popped up too. IE birthed the Trident browser engine and the TriEdit rendering/editing control. I used all of these things and more together to build applications that Netscape and Opera could not begin to do with their limited abilities. While history shows MS to be the bad guy, and I certainly have no love for them today with their latest series of anti-consumer practices, the truth is if you were needing to build big things then you did it with MS technologies. Yes it was anti-competitive, but when you work in a MS-centric company like I did, you didn't think about other options because they were not on the table.

Yes, today we have options, but back then you went with what worked. MS delivered that consistently (with some disasters mixed in too). I'm not defending them, but you have to admit at some point that we would not be where we are if these things hadn't happened. Enjoy the vast choice you have because it is built on the backs of those of us who had to give blood, sweat and tears in the proprietary world to make open source happen. I would argue, though, that open source has a long way to go and some maturing to do. I don't think we are doing enough and we need to work together to build better standards and support them for longer than the popularity time window we artificially put in place when something newer and shinier comes along.

I can't really think of any instance where I said something along the lines of "I'm happy with these microsoft products." They were always tinkering on the edge of instability and data loss. And still to this day.

Oh, how the times have changed. Office is losing its grip over the corporate and government world slowly but surely. I still find it funny how Microsoft calls their main format "Microsoft Office Open XML", when in reality it's not open at all. Other office suites struggle to render their documents to the level required by professional organizations.
